overview.title: Why overfitting happens: noisy training data
overview.section: 5.1 Generalization: The goal of machine learning
overview.main_topic: The first of three sources of overfitting: noisy training data (invalid inputs and mislabeled samples).
overview.central_idea: Overfitting is most likely when data is noisy, uncertain, or contains rare features. Real datasets like MNIST contain invalid inputs and mislabeled samples, and a model that bends itself to fit those outliers will generalize worse.
overview.importance: This page turns the abstract notion of overfitting from p.161 into something concrete: the training set itself contains garbage, and a model with enough capacity will faithfully learn that garbage. Knowing this explains why later remedies (dataset curation, regularization, early stopping) exist.
learning_objectives: List the three data conditions the book names as causes of overfitting: noise, uncertainty, rare features.
Distinguish two kinds of training-data noise: invalid inputs and mislabeled valid inputs.
Explain why fitting outliers degrades generalization, using the mislabeled-4 example.
Recognize that even a famous benchmark like MNIST is not perfectly clean.
prerequisites: Optimization vs. generalization and the definition of overfitting (p.161).

summary:
The page finishes the definition of overfitting started on p.161: once a model has overfit, it begins to learn patterns that are **specific to the training data** but misleading or irrelevant for new data. The authors then name the three situations in which overfitting is particularly likely: the data is **noisy**, it involves **uncertainty**, or it contains **rare features**. Each gets its own subsection; this page covers the first.

**Noisy training data.** Real-world datasets commonly contain *invalid* inputs. The book shows twelve strange MNIST training images (figure 5.2): blobs, scribbles, a heart-like shape, a cursive-looking stroke. Nobody, the authors included, can say which digit they are, yet they sit in the official training set with a label attached.

Worse are *perfectly valid* inputs carrying the *wrong label* (figure 5.3): a clear 4 labeled 9, a 1 labeled 7, a 7 labeled 4, a 9 labeled 3, and a 3 labeled 5 (the figure even prints each image's index in the training set, e.g. 14582 for the 4-labeled-9).

The consequence: if a model "goes out of its way" to incorporate such outliers, its generalization degrades (previewing figure 5.4 on p.163). Concretely, if the network memorizes that the mislabeled 4 is a "9", then a genuine test 4 that looks very similar may also be classified as a 9. The model has carved out a small region of input space around the bad sample and assigned it the wrong class.

The takeaway is that the training set is not ground truth; a sufficiently flexible model will learn its errors along with its signal, and that is one mechanism behind the validation-loss rise in figure 5.1 (p.161).

paragraphs.excerpt: learn patterns that are specific to the training data but that are
paragraphs.what_it_says: This is the end of a sentence begun on p.161: after enough training iterations, the model starts to overfit, that is, it begins to learn patterns specific to the training data that are misleading or irrelevant for new data.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Overfitting is defined behaviourally: the extra things the model learns late in training are not general rules of the task but quirks of this particular sample of data. They lower training loss without lowering (and eventually while raising) validation loss.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It frames everything on the following pages: each example (noise, ambiguity, rare features) is a different kind of training-set-specific pattern a model can latch onto.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Training loss keeps decreasing because the model can always reduce error on known points; the patterns that achieve the late decreases are those with no counterpart in the data-generating distribution.

terminology.meaning: The regime where improvements on training data no longer transfer, and eventually reverse, on unseen data.

connections: p.161: figure 5.1 shows the canonical curve where validation loss bottoms out and rises while training loss keeps falling.

paragraphs.excerpt: Overfitting is particularly likely to occur when your data is noisy,
paragraphs.what_it_says: Overfitting is especially likely when the data is noisy, involves uncertainty, or includes rare features; concrete examples follow.
paragraphs.what_it_means: This sentence is a roadmap for the rest of 5.1.1: 'Noisy training data' (this page), 'Ambiguous features' (p.163), and 'Rare features and spurious correlations' (p.164). In all three, the training data contains structure that does not reflect the real input-to-target relationship.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It tells you where to look when a model overfits: inspect the data for errors, for inherently ambiguous regions, and for rare or meaningless features.

terminology.meaning: Errors or randomness in inputs or labels that are not part of the true input-target relationship.
A feature value that appears in only a few training samples, so its apparent correlation with the target is unreliable.

connections: p.164: rare features and spurious correlations

paragraphs.excerpt: In real-world datasets, it’s fairly common for some inputs to be invalid.
paragraphs.what_it_says: Real datasets often contain invalid inputs; an MNIST digit could be an all-black image or something like the samples in figure 5.2.
paragraphs.what_it_means: An invalid input is one that does not actually belong to any class of the task, such as a blank image or a smudge, but it still has a label because every training sample needs one. Whatever label it carries is essentially arbitrary from the model's point of view.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Invalid inputs push the model to devote capacity to explaining samples that have no generalizable explanation.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Fitting an invalid sample means producing a confident prediction of its arbitrary label; the cheapest way for a network to do that is often to memorize that particular pixel pattern.

terminology.meaning: A sample that is not a legitimate instance of any target class (e.g. a blank or garbled image).

connections: p.183: dataset curation is discussed later as a way to improve generalization.

paragraphs.excerpt: What are these? We don’t know either. But they’re all part
paragraphs.what_it_says: The authors admit they cannot identify the figure 5.2 images either, yet all are in the MNIST training set. Worse still are valid inputs with the wrong label, shown in figure 5.3.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Two kinds of label noise are distinguished. Invalid inputs are confusing but at least unusual-looking, so they occupy odd corners of input space. Mislabeled valid inputs look exactly like normal digits of one class but carry another class's label, so they sit right in the middle of a class's region and directly contradict their neighbours.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: The second kind is more damaging because a model that memorizes it changes its predictions in a region where real test samples are dense. Figure 5.3 shows a 4 labeled 9, a 1 labeled 7, a 7 labeled 4, a 9 labeled 3 and a 3 labeled 5.

terminology.meaning: A valid input whose target in the dataset is incorrect.
Errors in the targets of a dataset.

connections: p.163: figure 5.4 shows geometrically how a model can contort its decision boundary around such points.

paragraphs.excerpt: If a model goes out of its way to incorporate such outliers,
paragraphs.what_it_says: A model that bends to fit such outliers loses generalization performance (figure 5.4); for instance, a 4 resembling the mislabeled 4 in figure 5.3 may be classified as a 9.
paragraphs.what_it_means: When the network memorizes the bad pair (image of 4, label 9), it effectively learns a rule like 'images very close to this one are 9s'. Test images near that point inherit the wrong answer. A robust model would instead accept a training error on the outlier and keep a simple boundary.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It shows that a lower training loss can be actively harmful: getting the mislabeled sample 'right' is equivalent to getting its look-alikes wrong.
paragraphs.technical_idea: A model that achieves zero training error on noisy labels must fit the noise; the gap between training accuracy and test accuracy then grows roughly with the fraction of noisy labels memorized.

terminology.meaning: A training point inconsistent with the general pattern of the data (here, invalid or mislabeled samples).
A model that captures the main trend and tolerates errors on outliers (term used in figure 5.4's caption, p.163).

connections: p.172: the book later stresses that adding noisy or inaccurate data harms generalization.

concepts.name: Overfitting
concepts.definition: The regime where a model learns patterns specific to its training data that are misleading or irrelevant for new data, so validation performance stalls and degrades while training performance keeps improving.
concepts.intuition: The model starts memorizing the answers to the practice exam, including the typos in the answer key.
concepts.technical: Driven by optimization minimizing empirical loss; once the general structure is captured, further loss reduction comes from fitting sample-specific idiosyncrasies (noise, ambiguity, rare features).
concepts.significance: The book calls the optimization/generalization tension the fundamental issue of machine learning (p.161); overfitting is its symptom.
concepts.example: A model memorizing that MNIST image #14582 (a clear 4) is a '9' and then misclassifying similar 4s.
concepts.misconception: Overfitting is not only about training too long; it is about what the model is fitting. Noisy data makes it happen sooner and more severely.

concepts.name: Label noise (mislabeled samples)
concepts.definition: Incorrect targets attached to otherwise valid training inputs.
concepts.intuition: An answer key with a few wrong answers: a student who memorizes it learns the mistakes too.
concepts.technical: With probability ε a sample's label is replaced by a wrong class. A high-capacity network can still reach ~100% training accuracy by memorizing these, but this cannot help, and generally hurts, test accuracy on look-alike inputs.
concepts.significance: Figure 5.3 shows that even the canonical MNIST benchmark has mislabeled samples.
concepts.example: Figure 5.3: a 4 labeled 9, a 1 labeled 7, a 7 labeled 4, a 9 labeled 3, a 3 labeled 5.
concepts.misconception: 'The labels in a benchmark are correct.' They are produced by humans and contain errors.

concepts.name: Noisy training data (invalid inputs)
concepts.definition: Training inputs that are not valid instances of any class, or otherwise corrupted, yet carry a label.
concepts.intuition: Smudges and doodles slipped into a stack of handwritten digits.
concepts.technical: Such samples have no consistent mapping to targets; fitting them forces the model to spend capacity on memorization.
concepts.significance: One of the three named causes of overfitting on this page.
concepts.example: Figure 5.2's twelve unidentifiable MNIST training images; a hypothetical all-black image.
concepts.misconception: Noise is not only random pixel noise; whole samples can be garbage.

concepts.name: Generalization
concepts.definition: How well a trained model performs on data it has never seen.
concepts.intuition: Passing the real exam, not the practice one.
concepts.technical: Measured as loss/metrics on held-out validation or test data drawn from the same distribution as the training data.
concepts.significance: The stated goal of machine learning in section 5.1; noisy data is one way to damage it.
concepts.example: A 4 in the test set should be predicted 4 even if a similar training 4 was mislabeled 9.
concepts.misconception: You cannot optimize generalization directly; you can only fit the training data (p.161).

deeper.title: Why a mislabeled point contaminates its neighbourhood
deeper.body:
Beyond the book, step by step:

1. A network maps similar inputs to similar outputs (it is a smooth, continuous function).
2. To output '9' for the mislabeled 4 (index 14582), it must push its output for that exact image towards class 9.
3. Because of smoothness, outputs for nearby images, other 4s written the same way, are dragged towards 9 too.
4. The size of the contaminated region depends on capacity and regularization: a very flexible model can make the region tiny (pure memorization, little harm), while a moderately flexible model may distort a larger area.
5. Either way, the decision boundary acquires a 'pocket' that does not correspond to anything real, which is exactly the right panel of figure 5.4 (p.163).

deeper.title: How common is label noise in benchmarks?
deeper.body: Note (not in the book): independent audits of popular datasets have found that a small fraction of labels are wrong, well under 1% for MNIST but several percent for some larger image and text benchmarks. Practical responses include re-labeling suspicious samples (those the trained model confidently disagrees with), using label smoothing, or using loss functions that down-weight samples with very high loss. The book's own remedy list on p.192 starts with 'getting more training data, or better training data'.

deeper.title: Answer key analogy
deeper.body: Imagine studying for a multiple-choice exam from a booklet whose answer key has a few typos. A good student notices that question 17's 'official' answer contradicts everything else they've learned and ignores it (a robust fit). A pure memorizer reproduces the typo, and also gives the wrong answer on the real exam to any question that looks like question 17.

visualizations.title: Flexible models chase noisy points
visualizations.why: The page warns that a model that 'goes out of its way to incorporate such outliers' generalizes worse. This regression analogue (a 1-D stand-in for the classification setting of figures 5.2-5.4) shows a high-degree fit bending through noisy training points while test error rises.

misconceptions.claim: Benchmark datasets like MNIST are perfectly clean.
misconceptions.correction: Figures 5.2 and 5.3 show unidentifiable and mislabeled images inside the MNIST training set.

misconceptions.claim: Reaching 100% training accuracy means the model is better.
misconceptions.correction: On noisy data, 100% training accuracy requires fitting the wrong labels, which degrades generalization (the mislabeled 4 example).

misconceptions.claim: Invalid inputs and mislabeled inputs are equally harmful.
misconceptions.correction: The book calls mislabeled valid inputs 'even worse', because they sit among real samples of a class and push the model's predictions there towards the wrong class.

earlier.note: Definition of optimization vs. generalization and figure 5.1's canonical overfitting curve; this page completes that paragraph.

later.note: Figure 5.4 (robust fit vs. overfitting around outliers) and the 'Ambiguous features' case.
Rare features and spurious correlations, the third named cause.
Deep models can fit even randomly shuffled labels, i.e. pure label noise.
Dataset curation as a way to improve generalization.
Recap: more or better training data is the first remedy against overfitting.

takeaways: Overfitting means learning training-set-specific patterns that are misleading for new data.
It is most likely with noisy data, uncertain/ambiguous data, or rare features.
MNIST contains invalid inputs (figure 5.2) and mislabeled valid inputs (figure 5.3).
Mislabeled valid inputs are worse than invalid ones because they contradict their neighbours.
Fitting an outlier, such as the 4 labeled 9, can cause similar test inputs to be misclassified.

questions.question: Name the three data conditions under which, according to the book, overfitting is particularly likely.
questions.answer: When the data is noisy, when it involves uncertainty (ambiguity), and when it includes rare features.
questions.explanation: Stated in the second paragraph of the page; each condition becomes its own subsection (noisy training data p.162, ambiguous features p.163, rare features p.164).

questions.question: Why does the book consider mislabeled valid inputs 'even worse' than invalid inputs?
options: They are more numerous in MNIST
They look like normal members of one class but carry another class's label, so fitting them corrupts predictions on similar real inputs
They cannot be loaded by Keras
questions.answer: They look like normal members of one class but carry another class's label, so fitting them corrupts predictions on similar real inputs
questions.explanation: The page's example: a 4 close to the mislabeled 4 may be classified as a 9. The book makes no claim about relative frequency; loading is irrelevant; and fitting them actually decreases training loss.

questions.question: A model reaches 100% training accuracy on a dataset with 2% wrong labels. What does that tell you about the model, and what would you expect on the validation set?
questions.answer: It has memorized the wrong labels as well as the correct ones, so it has fit noise. Validation accuracy will be lower than training accuracy, and inputs resembling mislabeled samples are at risk of being misclassified.
questions.explanation: A model can only be 100% right on wrong labels by reproducing them. Following the page's reasoning, this is 'going out of its way to incorporate outliers', which degrades generalization.

questions.question: In figure 5.3, which label is attached to the image that clearly shows a 4?
questions.explanation: The first image of figure 5.3 is a 4 labeled 9 (index 14582); the text uses it as the example. '7' is the label on the image of a 1, '4' is on the image of a 7, and '5' is on the image of a 3.

questions.question: Give an example of an 'invalid input' for MNIST mentioned in the text.
questions.answer: An all-black image (or the unidentifiable shapes in figure 5.2).
questions.explanation: The book says 'Perhaps a MNIST digit could be an all-black image, for instance—or something like figure 5.2.'

questions.question: Can you explain, without looking, why getting a mislabeled training sample 'right' can make a model worse?
questions.answer: Because the model's function is smooth, outputting the wrong class for that sample also shifts predictions for similar inputs towards the wrong class, so real test samples near it get misclassified.
questions.explanation: This is the mechanism behind the page's final sentence and figure 5.4's right panel (p.163).
